subject: Challonge
title: Challonge Alternatives in 2026
description: Eight tournament platforms to weigh against Challonge once an event outgrows a simple bracket: registration, prize pools, matchmaking and venue tools compared.
intro: Challonge is a tournament bracket service, and it is a common first stop for community organizers who need a bracket quickly. Its own site refused to open for our research fetcher, so this page makes no claim about its current features or prices; every statement below concerns the alternatives and comes from their own pages. The angle here is bigger events: the point where an organizer wants registration, ranking, prize pools, matchmaking or in-person venue tools around the bracket. Compare the options with the [esports tournament management software ranking](/software/best-esports-tournament-management-software) for the wider field.
why_switch: An event that has grown past one bracket often needs registration, rankings and a player profile around it, which platforms such as start.gg present as separate sections of the site.
Organizers who want to run a prize pool can look at Matcherino, which describes community-funded prize pools and payouts as part of its stack.
Teams that want automated matchmaking and gamification next to tournaments can look at Challengermode, which lists all three as its focus.
School and club programs may prefer a platform built around seasons for amateur players, which is how PlayVS describes its service.
Physical venues running LAN nights need booking and point of sale as well as brackets, a gap that ggLeap covers directly.

picks.name: start.gg
picks.pricing: No prices were readable on the site, which renders with JavaScript; confirm fees on the vendor page before committing.
picks.note: start.gg presents itself as a destination for creating, running, playing and watching tournaments, with rankings, shops and fantasy sections beside the tournament builder. That makes it the closest fit when an organizer wants players to find the event on a shared hub instead of a standalone bracket link. A developer portal is also linked. The trade-off is that a larger site means more setup choices than a single bracket page, and fees could not be read for this page.

sources.fact: start.gg describes itself as the leading destination to create, run, play and watch esports tournaments.
The start.gg site has sections for Create Tournament, Rankings, Shops and Fantasy.

picks.name: Battlefy
picks.pricing: The pricing page exists, but its text could not be read without JavaScript, so no prices are recorded here.
picks.note: Battlefy calls itself the simplest way to start, manage and find esports tournaments, so discovery is part of the pitch: players can find events as well as organizers creating them. It suits organizers who want sign-ups to come from a public listing. You give up the minimal feel of a bare bracket page, and you should read the pricing page yourself since its figures were not available to us.

sources.fact: Battlefy describes itself as the simplest way to start, manage and find esports tournaments.
The Battlefy pricing page loads without readable text, so no prices could be read.

picks.name: Toornament
picks.pricing: An organizer pricing page exists, but no prices were readable because the site renders with JavaScript.
picks.note: Toornament describes itself as having everything needed for esports competitions and runs an organizer pricing page titled as a solution for all competition projects. It is worth a look when a league or multi-stage cup needs more structure than a single bracket. The honest limit is detail: the home page content loads with JavaScript, so only the meta description could be read, and feature depth should be checked by trial.

sources.fact: Toornament's site describes itself as having everything needed for esports competitions.
The Toornament organizer pricing page is titled Organizers - A solution for all competition projects.

picks.name: Challengermode
picks.pricing: Free to start according to the site; developer pricing exists but its figures were not readable.
picks.note: Challengermode runs tournaments, matchmaking and gamification on one platform and says it covers more than 200 games across more than 80 countries. It is the pick for organizers who want players matched between events, not only a bracket on the day. Starting is free per the vendor, which lowers the cost of a trial, though the developer-side prices could not be read.

sources.fact: Challengermode describes itself as a competition management platform for gaming, running tournaments, matchmaking and gamification.
The Challengermode site says it is free to start.

picks.name: FACEIT
picks.best_for: Organizers inside a large player base
picks.pricing: Subscription packages are described in the help center; the figures were not in the text read.
picks.note: FACEIT has a help center written for organizers that covers tournament setup and clubs, and it publishes developer documentation as well. It fits organizers who want their events to sit inside an established competitive platform. The main site returned HTTP 403 to our fetcher, so subscription prices and the full feature list should be confirmed directly before choosing it.

sources.fact: The FACEIT help center is for organizers, covering how to set up tournaments and clubs.
The FACEIT help center has a section on subscriptions with information about its subscription packages.

picks.name: Matcherino
picks.pricing: Free organizer tools according to the site; prize pools are crowd-funded.
picks.note: Matcherino lets communities fund prize pools together and pairs that with free organizer tools for brackets, registration, payouts and sponsorships. For an event that depends on audience contributions, this is the most direct route. The model suits community cups more than closed internal leagues, and the pricing page text was not readable, so check any platform cut before you promote a pool.

sources.fact: Matcherino describes itself as a place to run and join esports tournaments with community-funded prize pools.
The Matcherino site describes free tools for organizers, including brackets, registration, payouts and sponsorships.

picks.name: PlayVS
picks.pricing: A PlayVS Essential option is listed; prices were not in the text read.
picks.note: PlayVS was founded in 2018 and positions itself as infrastructure for amateur competitive gaming, with program pages for high school, middle school and elementary school. If the real task is a school season with coaching tools and stats, it is a different shape from a bracket page. Open community brackets are not its focus, so skip it for drop-in weekend cups.

sources.fact: PlayVS was founded in 2018 and says it provides the infrastructure that powers amateur competitive gaming.
The PlayVS site lists high school, middle school and elementary school gaming programs.

picks.name: GGLeap
picks.pricing: Not published; the vendor asks prospects to request a demo.
picks.note: ggLeap is venue management software from ggCircuit, with PC booking, a player web portal, point of sale with Stripe payments, a coupon system and tournaments. It answers a different question from a bracket host: how to run the room itself. Choose it when your events happen in a gaming center. Online-only organizers will pay for features they never use, and pricing requires a demo request.

sources.fact: ggLeap is esports venue management software for gaming centers and LAN cafes, offered by ggCircuit.
ggLeap includes a PC booking system, a player web portal, a point of sale with Stripe payments and a coupon system.

how_to_pick: Start with where the event happens. An online open cup usually points to start.gg, Battlefy or Challengermode, because players can discover it. A cup funded by the audience points to Matcherino. A multi-stage league is worth a Toornament trial, and a school season belongs with PlayVS. A physical venue should look at ggLeap first. Because several vendors keep prices behind JavaScript or a demo, run one small free event on your shortlist before announcing a bigger one, and compare what registration looks like from the player side.

faqs.q: Why was Challonge not described in more detail here?
faqs.a: Its website blocked our research fetcher, so we could not open any page to verify features or pricing. Rather than repeat unchecked claims, this page limits itself to what each alternative says on its own pages. Check Challonge directly if you want a side-by-side on a specific feature.

faqs.q: Which alternative has a free way to start?
faqs.a: Challengermode says it is free to start, and Matcherino describes free tools for organizers. For the others, prices could not be read from the opened pages, so a trial event or a message to the vendor is the reliable way to learn what is free.

faqs.q: Is there an option for running a tournament in a physical venue?
faqs.a: ggLeap is built for gaming centers and LAN cafes and includes tournaments next to PC booking, loyalty and point of sale. It is overkill for an online-only organizer, but it replaces several tools for a venue.

faqs.q: What should a school or youth program consider?
faqs.a: PlayVS focuses on amateur gaming for schools, with program pages for high school, middle school and elementary school and coaching tools. Its structure is seasonal, so it suits a regular program better than a one-off event.

faqs.q: Can I fund a prize pool through the audience?
faqs.a: Matcherino describes community-funded prize pools with global payouts and free organizer tools. Verify its fees and payout rules on the vendor pages before advertising a pool, since the pricing text was not readable for this page.
